utterances.text: [Interpretation] Could we please bring up page 4.

utterances.speaker: MR. FILA
utterances.text: -- we can see that Sainovic joined the gathering, that he joined the work of the people attending?

utterances.speaker: MILOS VOJNOVIC
utterances.text: He came to that meeting just before the meeting ended, and as far as I remember, although it's been quite a long time, he addressed us with a couple of sentences, he greeted us, encouraged us a bit, and then left.

utterances.speaker: MR. FILA
utterances.text: Thank you. During the state of war, was it typical for high officials coming from Serbia and Yugoslavia to come and visit the army and the police, to address them with words of encouragement and so on?

utterances.speaker: MILOS VOJNOVIC
utterances.text: Yes, it was, and I can give you some examples. Mr. Seselj came on one occasion; and then minister of health at the time, I can't remember his name -- oh, it was Mr. Bojic; and then once there were also some visits from people from political parties, first of all, the SPS, I remember, say, Mr. Suvakovic, I don't remember his position.

utterances.speaker: MR. FILA
utterances.text: And did they all have a need to say something, to give a political statement, to get information about the events?

utterances.speaker: MILOS VOJNOVIC
utterances.text: The ones I mentioned, they came to the town of Prizren. Normally they went to see the chief of the Prizren district or they went to see people who were members of the local establishment. I usually attended those meetings myself.

utterances.speaker: MR. FILA
utterances.text: In other words, sir, I'm trying to ask you this: Was it typical or atypical for politicians at the republic level or high level to come and visit everybody because the country was at war?

utterances.speaker: MILOS VOJNOVIC
utterances.text: Yes, it was and those were our politicians, and also people came from abroad. Daniel Schaefer, I don't know what he was in international organizations, he came to Prizren during the war and he was even wounded.

utterances.speaker: MR. FILA
utterances.text: Thank you. Now, would you please look at the document that has already been shown to you, it's P1996, which is a meeting held at the MUP staff in Pristina on the 7th of May, 1999, you have it in your binder. Could you please find it.

utterances.speaker: MILOS VOJNOVIC
utterances.text: I have found it.

utterances.speaker: MR. FILA
utterances.text: As you can see, in the first sentence it says that vice prime minister of the federal cabinet of FRY, Mr. Sainovic, took part in the meeting. Do you see this?

utterances.speaker: MILOS VOJNOVIC
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. FILA
utterances.text: Do you remember that meeting, were you there?

utterances.speaker: MILOS VOJNOVIC
utterances.text: I was.

utterances.speaker: MR. FILA
utterances.text: Did he remain until the end, and while he was there what did he say?

utterances.speaker: MILOS VOJNOVIC
utterances.text: As far as I remember, he did not remain until the end. I think that at the very beginning and immediately when he came, he greeted us. He spoke about the situation, the war situation. I think he even drove our attention to the issue of abiding by the rule of law and abiding by professional rules of police, especially when it comes to perpetrators of crime, and I don't remember some other details. That's what I remember because this came within the sphere of work of our policemen.

utterances.speaker: MR. FILA
utterances.text: You might remember and you might not, but was there a communique submitted to you from the MUP staff with an excerpt from some daily?

utterances.speaker: THE INTERPRETER
utterances.text: Could Mr. Fila please speak into the microphone. The interpreters can't hear him.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I think that he spoke something about the communique or announcement that we had received earlier, it was from some papers, and this had been sent to us by the staff.

utterances.speaker: MR. FILA
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Could we see 5D1280 [as interpreted].

utterances.speaker: MR. FILA
utterances.text: And would you please continue once you see this document. 5D1289, 5D1289. You don't have it yet. Would you please look at page 1. Is this the information that you received concerning that article?

utterances.speaker: MILOS VOJNOVIC
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. FILA
utterances.text: [Interpretation] And could we now turn to page -- to the next page.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. FILA
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MR. FILA
utterances.text: So this is the article that Sainovic spoke about on that occasion, and you had already known about it because you had received it previously?

utterances.speaker: MILOS VOJNOVIC
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. FILA
utterances.text: Thank you. These two meetings where you had occasion to hear Sainovic, during these meetings did he convey to you some directives of the supreme commander or any other commander or anything of the sort?

utterances.speaker: MILOS VOJNOVIC
utterances.text: I did not understand him to convey anybody's directives to us, and there was no legal ground for that as far as I am aware of legislation in force.

utterances.speaker: MR. FILA
utterances.text: His presence and his words uttered at those two meetings, except for political meaning, as you said, did they have any other meaning, did they convey any order, any military content or what?

utterances.speaker: MILOS VOJNOVIC
utterances.text: I saw him as a high state official politician, that's how I perceived him.

utterances.speaker: MR. FILA
utterances.text: He was a federal official. You saw that it said there that he was vice prime minister of the federal government, and as far as I know you are a lawyer. Tell us, did federal government have any authority over MUP in 1998 or did MUP exist at the level of the republic and then you'll tell me the same thing concerning 1999.

utterances.speaker: MILOS VOJNOVIC
utterances.text: The federal MUP had no authority and it acted in accordance with the federal Law on Internal Affairs, whereas we at the republic level worked in accordance with the republic Law on Internal Affairs. So these are two separate organs of the interior, one at the federal level, one at the republic level.

utterances.speaker: MR. FILA
utterances.text: Would that mean, perhaps, that the federal cabinet had no authority over the work of the republic MUP, either in 1998 or in 1999?

utterances.speaker: MILOS VOJNOVIC
utterances.text: Precisely so.

utterances.speaker: MR. FILA
utterances.text: I apologise. You were shown a document a bit earlier and it mentions something like Joint Command in the heading. Let me ask you this: In that brief period of time in 1999 from the 11th of January or was it May or June that you stayed there in Prizren SUP, you were able to see within your chain of command in your contacts with colleagues above you, below you, at the same level as you, did you see the presence of anything known as the Joint Command, did you see it in a document? Did you hear about it ? Did you attend it? Did you participate in it in any way in 1999 while you were there?

utterances.speaker: MILOS VOJNOVIC
utterances.text: When it comes to the Joint Command, I didn't hear anything about the topic. For a while and in the beginning of the war it was said that there would be subordination of the police to the army; however, I didn't see that or experience it.

utterances.speaker: MR. FILA
utterances.text: My last question has to do with Cvetic again. At the MUP staff did you ever see a document that had come in with a heading of Joint Command in 1999?

utterances.speaker: MILOS VOJNOVIC
utterances.text: No.

utterances.speaker: MR. FILA
utterances.text: Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MR. FILA
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Thank you. That's all.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: Thank you, Mr. Fila. Mr. Bakrac.

utterances.speaker: MR. BAKRAC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Thank you, Your Honours.

utterances.speaker: MR. BAKRAC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Mr. Vojnovic, I'm Mihajlo Bakrac, attorney-at-law, I'm counsel for General Lazarevic, and I have just one question for certain; and depending on your answer I might have another one. Mr. Lukic asked you something about planning and you explained that you hadn't seen it, hadn't been involved in it.

utterances.speaker: MR. BAKRAC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Could we now see Exhibit P1505 that you have already seen, page 1, please.

utterances.speaker: MR. BAKRAC
utterances.text: You made a comment in examination-in-chief with Mr. Lukic about these persons who are listed here but actually did not take part in the work of the staff. I'm interested in this, under item 3, Radislav Djinovic, lieutenant-colonel, is mentioned. Was he in the staff?

utterances.speaker: MILOS VOJNOVIC
utterances.text: It's a very difficult question for me because I really spent only as much time at the staff as I needed for the meetings. I as a member of the MUP, I don't remember, and I know that Djinovic after leaving his post as chief of department in Serbia came to Pristina and worked there for a while. Now, as to whether he was a member of the staff in Pristina while I was there, I really wouldn't be able to tell you. I'm afraid I would make a mistake.

utterances.speaker: MR. BAKRAC
utterances.text: Thank you, Mr. Vojnovic. Just one more question. In this decision on establishing the staff, it says here that he was assistant head of staff for interventions and operations planning. Can you explain to us what operations planning means?

utterances.speaker: MILOS VOJNOVIC
utterances.text: I can give you my opinion, but I didn't socialise with Djinovic nor was I present when he planned anything. And if you want my understanding of this, then I took it that he probably had some information from the terrain, had some data that was of relevance for operations, but I remain by my initial answer.

utterances.speaker: MR. BAKRAC
utterances.text: Thank you very much, Mr. Vojnovic.

utterances.speaker: MR. BAKRAC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Your Honours, I have no further questions.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Thank you.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: Thank you, Mr. Bakrac. Mr. Vojnovic, you'll now be cross-examined by the Prosecutor, Mr. Hannis. Mr. Hannis.

utterances.speaker: MR. HANNIS
utterances.text: Thank you, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: MR. HANNIS
utterances.text: Good afternoon, Mr. Vojnovic. First, can I ask you to spell your last name for us. We've seen it spelled two or three different ways in various documents. I want to be sure we have it correctly on the record.

utterances.speaker: MILOS VOJNOVIC
utterances.text: It is written correctly on the statement that I signed, and I can show that to you, but I can also spell it letter by letter.

utterances.speaker: MR. HANNIS
utterances.text: No, I --

utterances.speaker: MR. HANNIS
utterances.text: Go ahead.

utterances.speaker: MILOS VOJNOVIC
utterances.text: V-o-j-n-o-v-i-c.

utterances.speaker: MR. HANNIS
utterances.text: Thank you. Can you tell me what work you were doing in the MUP between 1990 and 1998 before you were sent to Kosovo in January 1999?

utterances.speaker: MILOS VOJNOVIC
utterances.text: In 1990 I was assigned to work as commander of police station in the municipality of Savski Venac, Belgrade secretariat of the interior, where I remained for some two, two and a half years. After that I practically left the MUP, or rather, after that I went to the seat of the MUP to the police administration where I became chief of division for applying rule of law in work and training of members of police force, and I spent there less than a year, following which I was assigned to work in the post-secondary school of the interior as assistant chief for education administration. I spent there some two, two and a half years. Subsequently, I was appointed assistant chief of police administration in the seat of MUP.

utterances.speaker: MR. HANNIS
utterances.text: And was that the position you held when Minister Stojiljkovic told you you were going to be going to Prizren as the SUP chief, you were the assistant chief of police administration?

utterances.speaker: MILOS VOJNOVIC
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. HANNIS
utterances.text: And what were your duties as the assistant chief of police administration?

utterances.speaker: MILOS VOJNOVIC
utterances.text: Since I came to that post from the higher school of internal affairs, post-secondary school of internal affairs, my main task was to train and educate members of the police force.

utterances.speaker: MR. HANNIS
utterances.text: On what kinds of topics?

utterances.speaker: MILOS VOJNOVIC
utterances.text: When new employees are brought into service to the position of policeman, my work dealt with their applications and through the whole process until the moment they are sent to police courses and the curriculum at those courses and seminars or training sessions.

utterances.speaker: MR. HANNIS
utterances.text: Okay. Thank you. When you were the commander of the police station - and I can't pronounce the name - Savski Venac, how big a station was that? How many men did you have under you?

utterances.speaker: MILOS VOJNOVIC
utterances.text: Up to 140 policemen. It is a police station covering one part of Belgrade. In addition to Savski Venac and Vracar it is a central part of Belgrade, it fell under the department of the interior, Savski Venac.

utterances.speaker: MR. HANNIS
utterances.text: Thank you. You said you left that position after about two or two and a half years; was that at your request?

utterances.speaker: MILOS VOJNOVIC
utterances.text: We agreed on that.

utterances.speaker: MR. HANNIS
utterances.text: When Minister Stojiljkovic told you about being sent to Prizren, was that at your request or were you picked for the job?

utterances.speaker: MILOS VOJNOVIC
utterances.text: I was sent there without asking to be.

utterances.speaker: MR. HANNIS
utterances.text: Did he tell you why you were chosen for that job?

utterances.speaker: MILOS VOJNOVIC
utterances.text: I didn't dare ask him. He told me that my predecessor or the chief of the Prizren SUP is about to retire.

utterances.speaker: MR. HANNIS
utterances.text: In your personal view, was this a promotion or a lateral transfer or a demotion? How did you view it?

utterances.speaker: MILOS VOJNOVIC
utterances.text: There was very little time on my hands for me to ponder, but I certainly did not view that as a promotion. However, it wasn't to my detriment either. When we compare that to my previous post, it's about the same.

utterances.speaker: MR. HANNIS
utterances.text: Okay. Thank you. When was the first time you were aware of the existence of a body or a unit called the MUP staff of -- for Kosovo? When was the first time you ever heard of that?

utterances.speaker: MILOS VOJNOVIC
utterances.text: Mr. Prosecutor, this is a very difficult question for me. I can approximate, or rather, guess. In 1991 I was sent to Pristina. In 1992 I was appointed the head of the police course that was conducted in Vucitrn. Around that time there was a staff in existence, I don't know what kind of a staff it was, of a detachment or something else, but I cannot be any more precise now. I apologise.

utterances.speaker: MR. HANNIS
utterances.text: No, that's all right. I thank you for that. We have heard some other evidence in this trial about a MUP staff in Kosovo from the early 1990s. The reason I ask, though, is that that document that you were shown on direct testimony, that's Exhibit P1505, which is the 16 June 1998 decision of Minister Stojiljkovic establishing a staff. And I wanted to point out to you that that is to establish a ministerial staff for the suppression of terrorism, which is a longer name, a more specific name, than we've seen evidence about the earlier MUP staff. So did you notice that? Were you aware of that, that in 1998 this staff that was being created was specifically for the suppression of terrorism? Had you ever heard that term before or were you aware that that's how it was being referred to? Because I know you told us you didn't see the document before.

utterances.speaker: MILOS VOJNOVIC
utterances.text: I don't know if you'll be able to understand, but there was no need for me to know the full or the real name. For me it was a staff. What its full name was I truly cannot tell you precisely, as I don't know.

utterances.speaker: MR. HANNIS
utterances.text: And your early testimony today at page 9, line 13, you were asked if you had a duty to seek any kind of approval or consent from the MUP staff in order to engage your own units or units sent to the Prizren SUP to carry out tasks in your territory. Your answer was: "Practically speaking, there was no need for me to contact staff in relation to that." Even though there was no need to, did you, for whatever reason, contact the MUP staff about such things, about the engagement of units in your territory?

utterances.speaker: MILOS VOJNOVIC
utterances.text: I said that the sent units of the PJP, or rather, the detachment of the PJP that was sent there as well as the Prizren PJP company carried out regular tasks and assignments. It was done in agreement among the various lines of work at the ministry of the secretariat and the commander of the PJP. When I say "lines of work," I mean the chiefs of various departments, the police and other, including their deputies. When it comes to activities in which the PJP participated in terms of formations, a PJP company could be mobilised only pursuant to their own command's order, that is, the command of the intervention brigade from Pristina. As for the 37th PJP Detachment, it was mobilised, as far as I know, from or by the ministry itself, the MUP. There was a dispatch that came from MUP, I believe, and to be more specific it was probably done by the police administration.

utterances.speaker: MR. HANNIS
utterances.text: You were asked about a document or showing a meeting on the 4th of April, 1999, the MUP staff in Pristina, that's Exhibit P1989, and you were asked about a reference about mandatory reporting of chiefs of secretariats and unit commanders to staff. Did you -- I'm not clear, did you report regularly to MUP staff in Pristina after this 4th of April meeting where this mandatory reporting was brought up?

utterances.speaker: MILOS VOJNOVIC
utterances.text: I was appointed chief of the secretariat in January, as I've already told you. Practically speaking, there was no need for me to change anything by way of informing. Informing was in keeping with the guide-lines on informing and the circular which I believe was an annex to that information. I have to tell you that frequently we had no possibility to inform the MUP or the MUP staff since we had serious difficulties with communications, including the courier service. I think there were also other problems in terms of vehicles, fuel, and secure movement along the roads to Pristina and so on and so forth. As I usually say, most of it were extraordinary circumstances.

utterances.speaker: MR. HANNIS
utterances.text: Okay. You were asked about volunteers. Were you not aware of the presence of any Russian or Ukrainian volunteers in your area during the war?

utterances.speaker: MILOS VOJNOVIC
utterances.text: No.

utterances.speaker: MR. HANNIS
utterances.text: You --

utterances.speaker: MILOS VOJNOVIC
utterances.text: You have to understand, I was a chief of a secretariat. I mostly frequented the urban part of Prizren and the locations that were as they were. There I couldn't meet anything of the sort, and believe me when I say that I had no such information.

utterances.speaker: MR. HANNIS
utterances.text: You weren't aware of the existence of some sort of intervention unit that fought alongside elements of the 549th Motorised Brigade from the VJ and the 37th Detachment of the PJP that included Russian and Ukrainian volunteers? You didn't know about that?

utterances.speaker: MILOS VOJNOVIC
utterances.text: I didn't know about that. I had no such information.

utterances.speaker: MR. HANNIS
utterances.text: We had a discussion with you earlier today about the reserve police squads, and it wasn't clear to me at the end. You said in your statement that not -- that those were practically disbanded because during the war most of those people were mobilised either into the VJ or the MUP. But what about the ones who did not get mobilised into the VJ or the MUP, weren't they still around in late March or early April 1999 with the weapons they had been issued?

utterances.speaker: MILOS VOJNOVIC
utterances.text: Again, I have to stress that in practice while heading the secretariat I had no such problems or information of that nature. If I were to say anything it would be guess-work. I cannot tell you that they were without me knowing. In terms of the information I had, such people did not exist in the secretariat territory. When you say that some must have still been around, my guess is that General Lukic may have had certain information; but as for Prizren, the secretariat of the interior did not have such problems.

utterances.speaker: MR. HANNIS
utterances.text: You mention in your statement at paragraph 29 that: "Not a single mosque was damaged in Prizren itself." I take it you're talking about the town of Prizren itself, correct?

utterances.speaker: MILOS VOJNOVIC
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. HANNIS
utterances.text: How many mosques were there in Prizren town?

utterances.speaker: MILOS VOJNOVIC
utterances.text: I don't know whether you will accept my answer and I cannot be precise, but over 15.

utterances.speaker: MR. HANNIS
utterances.text: And you were aware that there were mosques in the municipality outside the town that were destroyed during the war, correct?

utterances.speaker: MILOS VOJNOVIC
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. HANNIS
utterances.text: Did you know about the one that was destroyed in Landovica?

utterances.speaker: MILOS VOJNOVIC
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. HANNIS
utterances.text: Your Honours, I'm about to move onto another topic. I don't know if this is a convenient time for our recess.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: It will be, Mr. Hannis. Mr. Vojnovic, we need a break at this stage, that for half an hour. While we have the break, would you please leave the courtroom with the usher.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: And we shall resume at 6.00.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: Mr. Hannis.

utterances.speaker: MR. HANNIS
utterances.text: Thank you, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: MR. HANNIS
utterances.text: Mr. Vojnovic, when you first got sent to Kosovo you told us you went down and met with your predecessor and spent a few days with him going over what your job would be like; correct?

utterances.speaker: MILOS VOJNOVIC
utterances.text: My predecessor was also sent from Belgrade. We left Belgrade together, that is what I said. He spent some time with me, two or three days.

utterances.speaker: MR. HANNIS
utterances.text: Let me --

utterances.speaker: MILOS VOJNOVIC
utterances.text: He was awaiting his retirement, handed over some things, and went back.

utterances.speaker: MR. HANNIS
utterances.text: And that was Gradimir Zekavica?

utterances.speaker: MILOS VOJNOVIC
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. HANNIS
utterances.text: Did he tell you that in the Prizren SUP they had adopted a plan to combat terrorism and that it was being implemented?

utterances.speaker: MILOS VOJNOVIC
utterances.text: No. If I may, I will repeat. I toured the various regional organizational units with him, and that was more or less it.

utterances.speaker: MR. HANNIS
utterances.text: Okay. Now, I wanted to ask you about the -- a couple more things in your statement before I move on to something else. With regard to the reporting regime that you described in your statement, you mentioned there were three kinds of reporting, there was urgent reporting, daily reporting, and periodic reporting. Which of those reports, if any, went to the MUP staff during your time there in 1999?

utterances.speaker: MILOS VOJNOVIC
utterances.text: Whenever it was possible to send a daily report to the MUP, we would also send it to the MUP staff in Pristina. It is an overview of events and occurrences with statistics.

utterances.speaker: MR. HANNIS
utterances.text: I will tell you, in order to try and save time, we have an exhibit in evidence here, it's Exhibit P1693. You don't have it in your folder, but it's a report or a summary dated the 1st of May, 1999, from the MUP staff to the Ministry of Internal Affairs in Belgrade. And it reports on the events in the area. And included within it at page 6 of the English and pages 3 and 4 of the B/C/S, there's a report about an event on the 30th of April, 1999, where members of the Prizren SUP had arrested -- I'm sorry, let me find it. I think I've got the wrong page reference. Sorry, it's page 8 of the English. On April 30th, officers of the Prizren SUP arrested and filed a criminal report against certain individuals for stealing a vehicle, et cetera. So it appears that at least on April 30th you were able to report to the MUP staff about a criminal arrest and report that had been filed in Prizren, and that's the kind of thing you would typically do; correct?

utterances.speaker: MILOS VOJNOVIC
utterances.text: It was on the 30th of April. At this moment I cannot recall the event. If it was registered, it must have happened, but as I said, when the war began - and we tied that to the beginning of air-strikes - at least concerning organization, it was difficult to function. As to the people who were drafting those reports and where they were sitting physically, I don't know. We used to call those locations wartime locations and we usually had contact at the level of leaders, leadership, and there was no direct communication between people who were supposed to do that as such.

utterances.speaker: MR. HANNIS
utterances.text: The last thing I wanted to ask you about from your statement is paragraph 43, you say: "I remember a case when some Albanians, several thousand of them withdrew to the mountains above Prizren during the bombing. When they decided to go to Albania, the representatives came to see me through the manager of the cinema and asked me to ensure safe passage for them to Albania. I told them there was no need for them to leave their homes and they should feel free to return. After this conversation, none of them showed up again." So you don't know what happened to those several thousand people?

utterances.speaker: MILOS VOJNOVIC
utterances.text: I don't know exactly what happened with them. It was just prior to the signing of the Kumanovo Agreement. I don't think any harm came their way.

utterances.speaker: MR. HANNIS
utterances.text: You --

utterances.speaker: MILOS VOJNOVIC
utterances.text: I apologise. I truly don't know.

utterances.speaker: MR. HANNIS
utterances.text: Okay. You were asked about anti-terrorist activity in the territory of your SUP and whether that was carried out under the control of the MUP staff. Your answer at page 10, line 20 today was: "As for anti-terrorist activities, we in SUP were in charge of that and PJPs." And then later on you said something else that left me somewhat unclear about who was in charge of those activities. You were asked about: "Was anybody's approval required in order for MUP units to be used?" And Mr. Lukic said: "I'm referring to PJP detachment and your company." And you said: "Not to my knowledge." The next question: "Was there any need to issue some special sorts of order to engage PJP units prior to each individual action?" And your answer was: "As far as I know, there was no need to do that; however, the PJP company of the Prizren SUP needed to get in touch with its command which was, I think, located in Pristina." So what was your role then as the chief of SUP in connection with the PJP units and anti-terrorist actions in 1999? Did you have any role?

utterances.speaker: MILOS VOJNOVIC
utterances.text: In the sense of control of PJP units, when they were involved in activities aimed at prevention of terrorist acts, I had no authorities there. However, when they were not involved in those tasks and duties but when they were doing their regular tasks and duties, then through a daily schedule of work they were assigned to regular duties, through regular modes of organization, which is check-points, patrols, beat policemen, and similar activities, detaining persons in town involving OPGs and so on.

utterances.speaker: MR. HANNIS
utterances.text: How did that work on a daily basis then? I mean, I suppose you wanted to have your men go out and do something in connection with the ordinary task of law enforcement, et cetera, and they didn't want to do that. Suppose they said, Oh, we can't do that today, boss, we have to go do some anti-terrorist action. How did you know whether that was real? Did someone from Pristina tell you, Oh, we need your PJP guys today for an anti-terrorist action, so please let them go? How did that work?

utterances.speaker: MILOS VOJNOVIC
utterances.text: That mostly functioned through the said senior officials of PJP, Colonel Mitrovic, Radenkovic, who was commander of the PJP in the Prizren SUP. Naturally there was certain problems in that area because if they were unable to perform regular duties and tasks, then that was additional strain for the remaining policemen who were not members of those units. Let me just mention an example of the type of additional strain or burden. They worked in two shifts, so instead of working for six hours and rest for 18 or 24 hours, they used to work for 12 hours and then rest for 12 hours.

utterances.speaker: MR. HANNIS
utterances.text: So between you and Colonel Mitrovic, then who had the higher authority or say about how those PJP personnel were going to be used? I mean, who decided whether they were going to be used for anti-terrorist actions and when and where and how? Who made that decision? Was that Colonel Mitrovic or somebody higher up?

utterances.speaker: MILOS VOJNOVIC
utterances.text: As chief of secretariat of the interior, I was unable to order anything to Colonel Mitrovic, and the same applied to him, he couldn't order anything to me. So he was the one who made decisions about his unit and I was in charge of the secretariat in Prizren.

utterances.speaker: MR. HANNIS
utterances.text: Did you and he ever have any conflict during 1999 about how individual members of the PJP were going to be used? I mean, was there ever a time when you really needed them to do some of your SUP work and he wanted to take them off on some anti-terrorist activity? Did that ever happen?

utterances.speaker: MILOS VOJNOVIC
utterances.text: I don't remember that Mitrovic and I had any sort of a conflict at any point in time on any topic.

utterances.speaker: MR. HANNIS
utterances.text: What about the 5th PJP Company, was that -- the PJP 5th Company from Prizren, was that under you or under Colonel Mitrovic or under somebody in Pristina in the brigade?

utterances.speaker: MILOS VOJNOVIC
utterances.text: When it comes to tasks aimed at prevention of terrorist acts, that company was under the command of Veljko Radenovic, its commander. Naturally I couldn't command it under those circumstances or in those cases. And I already told you that he had his superiors in the intervention brigade, the 124th one which was headquartered in Pristina.

utterances.speaker: MR. HANNIS
utterances.text: You mentioned at page 36 today that before activities were carried out, you would receive a map normally from the commander of the PJP company from Prizren or from Colonel Mitrovic. How far in advance of the planned activities would you receive a map, would it be a day or two ahead of time or the same day, do you recall?

utterances.speaker: MILOS VOJNOVIC
utterances.text: I think a day, perhaps two days, prior to that, not earlier than that.

utterances.speaker: MR. HANNIS
utterances.text: Do you ever recall seeing on any of those maps you received the word "Joint Command"?

utterances.speaker: MILOS VOJNOVIC
utterances.text: I truly don't remember seeing anything of that sort, and I have already said that when it comes to those coded maps and markings on them, it was important for me to the extent that it indicated whether I had any duties when it comes to logistics and assistance that was needed on the ground in that sense.

utterances.speaker: MR. HANNIS
utterances.text: You mentioned today at page 36 that you -- "almost daily General Delic, myself, the commander of the 37th Detachment saw each other and spent time together." And you were asked about coordination. You said: "It's difficult for me to grasp the concept of coordination. They didn't hide any of their conversations from me. I did not participate in the creation of this plan. I didn't decide on when activities were to be undertaken." And you told us that mostly you met in the barracks, within the barracks in Prizren at the PJP commander's office. General Delic, I guess he was then Colonel Delic, testified in this trial on the 29th of November. And at page 19344 of the transcript he was asked this question by Mr. Cepic: "Who did you cooperate with most frequently from the MUP?" And his answer was: "On the territory of Prizren municipality there is a secretariat of the interior and I cooperated usually with the chief of the secretariat, in 1998 that was Colonel Zekavica, in 1999 that was Colonel Milos Vojinovic" is how he said it, but I'm sure he meant you, Vojnovic, corrected? Even though in the transcript they had it spelled as Vojinovic, but there was only one colonel in charge of the SUP, that was you, right?

utterances.speaker: MILOS VOJNOVIC
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. HANNIS
utterances.text: And then he said: "They were my counterparts more or less when we were carrying out coordination the commander of the 37th Detachment, Colonel Mitrovic, would be called to the secretariat in Prizren, and in the secretariat we would meet. On the maps we would specify how both sets of forces were to act." Now, that's different than what you told us. Do you disagree with Colonel Delic, that you -- the three of you met in the secretariat to discuss these maps and how the forces would act?

utterances.speaker: MILOS VOJNOVIC
utterances.text: I have said that when there was opportunity for us to meet, we would meet on a daily basis, and I'm mostly referring to the time before the bombing began. As I said, most often we would meet in the barracks because the command of the 37th Detachment of PJP was headquartered in the barracks as well as the command of the Army of Yugoslavia. On those occasions we discussed many duties and obligations, and everything functioned well among us. We were like brothers. All of us knew our own obligations.

utterances.speaker: MR. HANNIS
utterances.text: Okay.

utterances.speaker: MILOS VOJNOVIC
utterances.text: I didn't know nor was I duty-bound to know --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: The question is: Where did you meet? And Mr. Hannis asked you if you disagreed, if you disputed the evidence given by Delic, that's all.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Your Honours, I apologise. If possible I wanted to explain this in greater detail, the situation. As I said, most often in the barracks, but we would also meet in my offices and also in the premises of the municipality and so on.

utterances.speaker: MR. HANNIS
utterances.text: And do you disagree with him that you would discuss on the maps how both sets of forces were going to act? That's what the three of you did, right?

utterances.speaker: MILOS VOJNOVIC
utterances.text: The three of us didn't do that. I was in charge of the secretariat in Prizren in charge of regular duties and tasks. Prevention of terrorist acts is not a regular task, nor was it performed by regular police forces, except when they were forced to do that, when they were attacked. So I wasn't able to participate in the drafting of the plan because I didn't know how to do that, but naturally we talked. I had many other tasks in relation to that.

utterances.speaker: MR. HANNIS
utterances.text: You answered my question. You said at page 39, line 12 today: "Of course we discussed the activities of the Siptar terrorist forces, we discussed our duties and obligations concerning carrying out joint patrols and joint check-points, we discussed those taken into custody and other things." During those joint VJ/MUP anti-terrorist activities, do you recall any prisoners actually having been taken by units of the 549th and the 37th PJP Detachment? Can you recall any?

utterances.speaker: MILOS VOJNOVIC
utterances.text: This is a difficult question for me. You have to allow me to give an explanation. The term "prisoner" is not clear to me as a policeman. The police could only have detained persons and the police did have them --

utterances.speaker: MR. HANNIS
utterances.text: Well, let me stop you there. Did -- after any of these joint VJ and MUP anti-terrorist activities, did they bring in anybody alive?

utterances.speaker: MILOS VOJNOVIC
utterances.text: Naturally.

utterances.speaker: MR. HANNIS
utterances.text: And can you tell --

utterances.speaker: MILOS VOJNOVIC
utterances.text: I just remembered, I think that one person wearing a uniform of a Siptar terrorist group was brought in, I'm not sure about the date, but it was the action in Jeskovo, not that I think, I'm sure about that because I was informed about that by my subordinates from the service where that person was detained and later charges were filed and he was handed over to competent authorities.

utterances.speaker: MR. HANNIS
utterances.text: If I'm not mistaken, if that was the action in Jeskovo village sector, that took place on or about the 11th of March, 1999, correct?

utterances.speaker: MILOS VOJNOVIC
utterances.text: Yes, that was in March.

utterances.speaker: MR. HANNIS
utterances.text: Okay. Could we take a look at Exhibit P1998, and I can give you a hard copy, Mr. Vojnovic. This is a --

utterances.speaker: MILOS VOJNOVIC
utterances.text: Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MR. HANNIS
utterances.text: I doubt that you've seen this before. This is a report by Colonel Delic, an after-action report on the joint anti-terrorist activity in Jeskovo village sector that took place on the 11th of March. It's dated 12 March 1999, and among the things he reports it's -- at the top of page 2 of the English and it's near the bottom of page 1 for you, I think I've highlighted it in pink. And he gives his estimate of the Siptar terrorist losses. He indicates: "Nine killed, no one was captured." Now, having read that, does that refresh your memory that perhaps you're mistaken about when a captured terrorist was brought in after anti-terrorist activities?

utterances.speaker: MILOS VOJNOVIC
utterances.text: Mr. Prosecutor, I apologise to you, but I wouldn't consider myself entitled to interpret the regulations and documents of the Army of Yugoslavia. I don't know what kind of terms they use and I don't want to speculate. I can tell you about the Law on Internal Affairs and I can tell you about the Law on Criminal Procedure which regulate in great detail these topics. So what exactly General Delic wrote in this particular case is something you need to ask him.

utterances.speaker: MR. HANNIS
utterances.text: Well, really, and we did. But, Mr. Vojnovic, there's nothing complicated about that language. It says: "Nine killed, no one was captured." What is it about that that you can't understand? That means no prisoners were taken, right? Prisoners, detainees, capturees, whatever you want to call them, no one was brought in alive, right?

utterances.speaker: MILOS VOJNOVIC
utterances.text: No, that's not how it was. Now you're reminding me of some other things. Since this activity was carried out in daylight, throughout the day, and we knew that there were persons who were killed, together with the observers of the OSCE we secured that entire area or the majority of that area. And together with them on the following day we conducted an on-site investigation. I can't really remember the exact number. I know that persons were killed, but there's no need for me to speculate because there is the record of the investigation conducted on site and I suppose that there are also members of that mission who were there on site. I even remember that there was a policeman from the German police who had been sent and who took part in that on-site investigation so --

utterances.speaker: MR. HANNIS
utterances.text: Let me stop you there. You're not answering my question. Let's move on to something else. If you would go down from that paragraph under item number 2 it talks about the forces engaged in this operation, and you'll see it identifies the MUP forces as being the 5th PJP Company of Prizren and the 37th PJP Detachment of a strength of about 300 men. And you don't have any disagreement with that, right, you knew those forces from Prizren were involved in this anti-terrorist action, right?

utterances.speaker: MILOS VOJNOVIC
utterances.text: With your permission, prior to the beginning of bombing the entire --

utterances.speaker: MR. HANNIS
utterances.text: Are you --

utterances.speaker: MILOS VOJNOVIC
utterances.text: -- PJP detachment from Nis --

utterances.speaker: MR. HANNIS
utterances.text: Excuse me, sir, are you trying to answer my question?

utterances.speaker: MILOS VOJNOVIC
utterances.text: I don't know how many there were. I apologise, but I cannot confirm this figure.

utterances.speaker: MR. HANNIS
utterances.text: Okay. But although you may not be able to confirm the figure, you can confirm the units, that parts of the 5th PJP Company and the 37th PJP Detachment took place in this joint activity, anti-terrorist activity, with the VJ on the 11th of March in the Jeskovo village sector, right?

utterances.speaker: MILOS VOJNOVIC
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. HANNIS
utterances.text: And while we're at it let me show you one more related document, this is P1999, and with the usher's help I'll trade you documents. This is dated the 18th of March, 1999, also from Colonel Delic of the 549th, and it's reporting on the activities on the 17th of March in the Kabas village sector, which I think you mentioned earlier in your testimony. You'll see near the bottom of your page 1, and for us in English it's on -- near the top of page 2. We'll scroll down to the bottom for you in a second. There's an estimate of the number of losses of the Siptar terrorists, and here it says 11 were killed and no one was captured. And further down in item 2 regarding the forces involved, you'll see it mentions MUP forces engaged were the 5th PJP Company of Prizren and the 37th PJP Detachment of Nis, here this time with a strength of about 350 men. Now, I understand you may not be able to confirm the number of men, but you were aware that those two units were engaged in this anti-terrorist action with the 549th on the 17th of March in the Kabas village sector, right?

utterances.speaker: MILOS VOJNOVIC
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. HANNIS
utterances.text: On both of these occasions, the 11th and 17th of March actions, had you seen a copy of the map regarding those proposed actions before they took place?

utterances.speaker: MILOS VOJNOVIC
utterances.text: Except for what I mentioned earlier, the coded maps, I did not see it on A4 format, hard copy. I apologise. I remember these events well. I was in the town of Prizren throughout that whole time.

utterances.speaker: MR. HANNIS
utterances.text: Okay. I wasn't clear from your testimony. I understand --

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: I apologise for a second.

utterances.speaker: MR. HANNIS
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: I think that the witness said that he did see it on the A4 format, not that he didn't see it on the A4 format.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: Perhaps you should check that with the witness, Mr. Hannis. Thank you, Mr. Lukic.

utterances.speaker: MR. HANNIS
utterances.text: Mr. Vojnovic, did you hear that and can you tell us which it was, did you or did you not see the map on A4 format?

utterances.speaker: MILOS VOJNOVIC
utterances.text: I saw the map in A4 format.

utterances.speaker: MR. HANNIS
utterances.text: For both of those actions in Jeskovo and Kabas? I guess was it two separate maps or did -- that you saw on two separate occasions?

utterances.speaker: MILOS VOJNOVIC
utterances.text: Yes, yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. HANNIS
utterances.text: Thank you. Let me move onto something different for the moment. I'd like to show you Exhibit P1723. I don't know if you will have seen this document before or not because it's another VJ document. It's dated the 24th of May, 1999. With the usher's help I'll trade you. This is a report from Colonel Lazarevic, and I'm showing it to you in connection to your answer about joint patrols and joint check-points. You indicated that in Prizren and other towns in your area you had both joint patrols and check-points. First of all, is that correct, in 1999 did you have joint patrols and check-points with the VJ?

utterances.speaker: MILOS VOJNOVIC
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. HANNIS
utterances.text: And that also included during the war after the bombing started?

utterances.speaker: MILOS VOJNOVIC
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. HANNIS
utterances.text: I want to ask you about paragraph -- I think it's the sixth paragraph, and for you I think it's the second one from the bottom on the screen in front of you now. I'll read from my English translation. It says: "The work of mixed check-points of the MUP and the military police units is fraught with problems and salient issues since the MUP tolerates criminal activities of its members against the Siptar civilian population - murder, rape, looting, robbery, aggravated theft ..." Did anybody in the army or outside the army complain to you about these kind of problems at joint check-points with the VJ prior to the 24th of May, 1999?

utterances.speaker: MILOS VOJNOVIC
utterances.text: As far as I remember, no.

utterances.speaker: MR. HANNIS
utterances.text: Thank you. With regard to the 5th PJP Company, where did they -- where were they housed or where did they stay when they were not engaged in activities in the field? Were they at the SUP or at the barracks or where were they?

utterances.speaker: MILOS VOJNOVIC
utterances.text: I apologise, what do you mean where were they? Can you explain that? While they were working or what?

utterances.speaker: MR. HANNIS
utterances.text: Where were they housed? Was there a place where they stayed or were these just regular policemen who went home at the end of the day? Did they have some kind of compound or barracks or housing unit?

utterances.speaker: MILOS VOJNOVIC
utterances.text: Precisely what you said. After work they would go home.

utterances.speaker: MR. HANNIS
utterances.text: I understood the 37th PJP Detachment was housed at the barracks where the 549th was, is that correct, for them?

utterances.speaker: MILOS VOJNOVIC
utterances.text: You mean members of PJP in Prizren?

utterances.speaker: MR. HANNIS
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MILOS VOJNOVIC
utterances.text: I apologise.

utterances.speaker: MR. HANNIS
utterances.text: Member -- PJP members of the 37th Detachment.

utterances.speaker: MILOS VOJNOVIC
utterances.text: They were billeted in the barracks until the commencement of air-strikes, when they left the location, as we all did.

utterances.speaker: MR. HANNIS
utterances.text: Okay. And after that where were they housed when they weren't in action? Did they have a single location or did they move around from place to place because of the bombing?

utterances.speaker: MILOS VOJNOVIC
utterances.text: Mr. Prosecutor, it is difficult for me to tell you where they were, maybe out in the open. I truly don't know.

utterances.speaker: MR. HANNIS
utterances.text: Okay.

utterances.speaker: MILOS VOJNOVIC
utterances.text: For me they were somewhere in the field.

utterances.speaker: MR. HANNIS
utterances.text: Okay. Thank you. You told us earlier today that you worked at the disciplinary court of the MUP of Serbia, first at the first-instance court and then the next level up; and you also worked as a prosecutor and a member of the chamber and president of the court. But during what time-period was all that? Was that throughout your career or just a certain time-period?

utterances.speaker: MILOS VOJNOVIC
utterances.text: Throughout my career. When I entered the service and until one or two months prior to my retirement.

utterances.speaker: MR. HANNIS
utterances.text: Did you engage in any of that activity in 1999?

utterances.speaker: MILOS VOJNOVIC
utterances.text: I apologise. I wasn't always at this highest position, I was also a member of chambers.

utterances.speaker: MR. HANNIS
utterances.text: I understand. Did you do any work with the disciplinary court in any one of those roles in 1999?

utterances.speaker: MILOS VOJNOVIC
utterances.text: Since I was appointed chief of the SUP and by the virtue of that fact alone I was a part of the disciplinary procedure.

utterances.speaker: MR. HANNIS
utterances.text: Let me ask you about a few of the MUP meetings that you attended during your time as SUP chief. The first one I wanted to ask you about is Exhibit P1990, a meeting on the 17th of February, 1999. I can hand you a hard copy. You talked about this before, and I think I only had one question for you on this meeting. Do you recall attending this one where Minister Stojiljkovic attended and addressed the group?

utterances.speaker: MILOS VOJNOVIC
utterances.text: I do recall.

utterances.speaker: MR. HANNIS
utterances.text: And on page 3 of the B/C/S, I'm not sure -- I may have marked it --

utterances.speaker: MR. HANNIS
utterances.text: And that's page 5 of the English, Your Honours, and my learned friends.

utterances.speaker: MR. HANNIS
utterances.text: -- Stojiljkovic says: "We are counting on phases of pressure. Within two or three days of an attack we have to put our plans in motion and use the time to mop up the territory from terrorists." Do you remember him talking about that? I'm sorry if -- I think it's on page 3 of the B/C/S and it's right above -- there's a series of bullet points. It's the paragraph right before the bullet points start. I don't know if the usher can assist.

utterances.speaker: MILOS VOJNOVIC
utterances.text: I found it.

utterances.speaker: MR. HANNIS
utterances.text: Okay. Yeah.

utterances.speaker: MILOS VOJNOVIC
utterances.text: If I may.

utterances.speaker: MR. HANNIS
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MILOS VOJNOVIC
utterances.text: Can you repeat the question, please?

utterances.speaker: MR. HANNIS
utterances.text: Do you recall him saying these words or words to this effect, about: We have to put our plans in motion and use the time to mop up the territories from the terrorists within two or three days of being attacked, and I can tell you from the earlier he's talking about NATO. Do you recall that?

utterances.speaker: MILOS VOJNOVIC
utterances.text: To be honest, I don't remember that.

utterances.speaker: MR. HANNIS
utterances.text: Okay.

utterances.speaker: MILOS VOJNOVIC
utterances.text: Knowing the minister, though, I would say these were his words.

utterances.speaker: MR. HANNIS
utterances.text: Okay. Isn't it correct that there was a plan that if NATO attacked you all were going to try to destroy or get rid of as many KLA as possible during that time before a NATO ground invasion took place? Wasn't that part of the general plan, if you know?

utterances.speaker: MILOS VOJNOVIC
utterances.text: I don't know that we had such a plan, at least I didn't see it.

utterances.speaker: MR. HANNIS
utterances.text: Okay. Thank you. Let me then ask you about a meeting on the 4th of April, 1999, this is in Exhibit P1989 and I can give you a hard copy of this one. I think you were shown this one before as well. You attended the meeting and we see you speaking at page 2 of both the English and the B/C/S. Do you find that, where you're speaking, sir?

utterances.speaker: MILOS VOJNOVIC
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. HANNIS
utterances.text: You mentioned 19 persons being taken in custody, problems with Muslims and Turks leaving, and unburied bodies in the zone of anti-terrorist activities. How big a problem was that for you? How many unburied bodies were you talking about here, five or six or dozens or what?

utterances.speaker: MILOS VOJNOVIC
utterances.text: I cannot answer precisely; however, as the chief of SUP I did have certain problems with corpses. There were cattle, corpses of people. There was a problem that was particularly acute. In Pusto Selo, which was within the territory of our SUP, we had information that a number of corpses had been buried there. Since we were duty-bound to investigate, we needed to check the information; however, it proved to be very difficult if I remember correctly. We went there once; however, we didn't manage to arrive at the destination due to Siptar terrorist activities. We went out for a second time and I believe it was with the assistance of certain VJ units --

utterances.speaker: MR. HANNIS
utterances.text: I'm sorry to interrupt you, sir. I was just asking about the numbers if you could tell us. Also on that page could you go down where you see a reference to Radislav Mitrovic, the PJP 37th Detachment commander. He notes in the second point that: "Situation in units is good as well as cooperation with the VJ and the secretariat." And I think you agreed with that; you told us that you in the secretariat had good cooperation with the 37th PJP, right?

utterances.speaker: MILOS VOJNOVIC
utterances.text: That is right.

utterances.speaker: MR. HANNIS
utterances.text: And I think two last things I want to ask you about on this document, if you could go to the last page. And we have Obrad Stevanovic speaking. You see the last bullet point under him is: "Conduct cooperation with the VJ through the commander on the ground and inform the staff of any problems." You were doing that, right? You were cooperating with the VJ through the commander, Colonel Delic, and you didn't have any problems that you needed to report to the staff, did you?

utterances.speaker: MILOS VOJNOVIC
utterances.text: I don't remember. I don't think I had any problems with Colonel Delic.

utterances.speaker: MR. HANNIS
utterances.text: And from that one that we just read can you go up one, two, three bullet points. There's one that says: "Control and command of units in the area of a secretariat is done by the chiefs." Can you explain to us what that means in light of what you've said about the PJPs and how they were directed in the area of your secretariat? Those two things don't seem to match up, what you told us before and what Stevanovic is saying here.

utterances.speaker: MILOS VOJNOVIC
utterances.text: Excuse me, which bullet point?

utterances.speaker: MR. HANNIS
utterances.text: Well, from the one that we just read, if you went up three above it or if you started at the top of the page under Stevanovic and went down one, two, three, four -- six --

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: I'm sorry.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: Mr. Lukic.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: I think this is asked and answered during the direct examination.

utterances.speaker: MR. HANNIS
utterances.text: Well --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: Thank you. That doesn't matter. It's still within Mr. Hannis's province if he wishes to cross-examine on that. Mr. Hannis.

utterances.speaker: MR. HANNIS
utterances.text: Yes, I would.

utterances.speaker: MR. HANNIS
utterances.text: Did you find it, Mr. Vojnovic?

utterances.speaker: MILOS VOJNOVIC
utterances.text: I did.

utterances.speaker: MR. HANNIS
utterances.text: Okay. And my question was: This is coming from General Stevanovic, who I understood was sort of the ministry guy in charge of PJPs, and he's saying: "Control and command of units in the area of a secretariat is done by the chiefs." That seems to be in conflict with what you told us about how the PJPs were commanded in the area of your secretariat. Can you explain that for us?

utterances.speaker: MILOS VOJNOVIC
utterances.text: I said several times today that I controlled the units of the police from the regular, from among the regular forces and when they performed regular tasks. In this case General Obrad Stevanovic had that in mind in particular. This order of his did not authorise me to undertake any control over PJP units.

utterances.speaker: MR. HANNIS
utterances.text: What was General Stevanovic's job in the ministry at this time, do you know?

utterances.speaker: MILOS VOJNOVIC
utterances.text: As far as I know, General Stevanovic was assistant minister. I believe he also was at the position of the police administration chief at the seat of the ministry.

utterances.speaker: MR. HANNIS
utterances.text: Was there anybody at the ministry other than the minister himself who had greater control over PJP units in the Republic of Serbia than General Stevanovic, if you know?

utterances.speaker: MILOS VOJNOVIC
utterances.text: As far as I know, minister and sector chiefs were General Stevanovic's superiors.

utterances.speaker: MR. HANNIS
utterances.text: With regard to the PJP?

utterances.speaker: MILOS VOJNOVIC
utterances.text: Excuse me. I don't know their relationships.

utterances.speaker: MR. HANNIS
utterances.text: Well, other than Minister Stojiljkovic and General Djordjevic, as head of the public security sector, was there anybody between them and General Stevanovic in terms of a chain of command over the PJP units in the Republic of Serbia in 1999; and if so, who was that person?

utterances.speaker: MILOS VOJNOVIC
utterances.text: I don't think there was such a person.

utterances.speaker: MR. HANNIS
utterances.text: Thank you. Then I need to go to P1996, which is a meeting of the 7th of May and this is one that I think you were shown earlier as well. This is a long one. I'll hand you a hard copy.

utterances.speaker: MILOS VOJNOVIC
utterances.text: I found it.

utterances.speaker: MR. HANNIS
utterances.text: Oh, okay. You have it. That's fine if you have it. I want to take you first to page 6 of the B/C/S, and it's page 7 in the English. This is where you are speaking, and you talked a little bit about this. If you could go down -- well, go down six bullet points, where you're talking about 61 persons were brought into the court but inaccurate sentences were pronounced. Do you find that? I think you told us about that before.

utterances.speaker: MILOS VOJNOVIC
utterances.text: I found it.

utterances.speaker: MR. HANNIS
utterances.text: And right below that you say: "A judge was detained; however, he was released from detention because he purportedly received call-up papers and was supposed to go to the front." Do you recall what that judge was detained for?

utterances.speaker: MILOS VOJNOVIC
utterances.text: I think he was a judge with the municipal court in Prizren. His name is Bakic or something that sounds like it. I don't know what his first name is. As far as I recall, he was found committing the act of illicit trade together with some other people. I don't know exactly, but I think there was a criminal report filed against him and others and you can verify that. That's what I can recall offhand. As for his call-up papers, it was merely a story. I think he was in detention, but he disappeared. He hailed from Montenegro and the rumour had it that he left for Montenegro. Another rumour would have us believe that he was on a different task. As far as I remember, while I was in Prizren I did not manage to establish his whereabouts.

utterances.speaker: MR. HANNIS
utterances.text: Okay. Let me ask you one more question before we break for the evening then -- well, two questions. One, it sounds like you think there was something shady or perhaps improper about his being released; is that correct?

utterances.speaker: MILOS VOJNOVIC
utterances.text: I have to tell you that at that time I was also in the capacity of a policeman of sorts and I had my reasons to suspect that.

utterances.speaker: MR. HANNIS
utterances.text: Okay.

utterances.speaker: MILOS VOJNOVIC
utterances.text: However, I had no proof.

utterances.speaker: MR. HANNIS
utterances.text: I understand --

utterances.speaker: MILOS VOJNOVIC
utterances.text: Had I had it, I would have brought him back.

utterances.speaker: MR. HANNIS
utterances.text: The very next bullet point it says: "In connection with this a meeting with the judges was held and they were warned about such conduct." First of all, who met with the judges, was that you?

utterances.speaker: MILOS VOJNOVIC
utterances.text: I think this is imprecise or maybe I was imprecise when speaking, with the representatives of the court and the prosecutor's office, this is who I met with, the president of the court and the prosecutor, that is.

utterances.speaker: MR. HANNIS
utterances.text: Your Honours, if I may take two more minutes to finish this point.

utterances.speaker: MR. HANNIS
utterances.text: And what was the warning that was given to the judges? What was the nature of the warning?

utterances.speaker: MILOS VOJNOVIC
utterances.text: It is certain that I had no right to warn because courts are supposed to be independent. I asked them. Maybe when reporting I used the word to warn or it was merely the recorder who noted that down. If you're interested in the relation between the SUP and the prosecutor's office, we are in no position to issue orders to each other.

utterances.speaker: MR. HANNIS
utterances.text: I understand --

utterances.speaker: MILOS VOJNOVIC
utterances.text: And I never did.

utterances.speaker: MR. HANNIS
utterances.text: Let me stop there then.

utterances.speaker: MR. HANNIS
utterances.text: Your Honours, may we break there for the evening.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: Mr. Vojnovic, we have to break there for this evening and resume tomorrow. You will, I'm afraid, require to return here to complete your evidence tomorrow afternoon at 2.00 -- sorry, 2.15. Between now and then it is a strict rule that you should have no communication with anyone, anyone at all, about the evidence in this case or any aspect of the evidence in this case. Now could you please leave the courtroom with the usher and we'll see you again tomorrow at 2.15.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: to be reconvened on Thursday, the 13th day of March, 2008, at 2.15 p.m.

procedural_notes.text: --- Whereupon the hearing adjourned at 7.03 p.m.
